title: Attributes and reflection
body: Attributes attach metadata to code: `[Obsolete("use V2")]`, `[Flags]`, `[JsonPropertyName("id")]`. They do nothing by themselves; the compiler, the runtime, frameworks or your own code read them. Define your own by deriving from `Attribute` and restrict where it may appear with `[AttributeUsage]`.

Reflection inspects types at runtime: `typeof(T)` or `obj.GetType()` returns a `Type`, from which you can list properties, methods and attributes, read and write values, and invoke members. Serializers, test runners, dependency-injection containers and ORMs rely on it.

Reflection is slow compared with direct calls, bypasses compile-time checking and breaks when code is trimmed or compiled ahead of time (Native AOT), because the trimmer cannot see which members are used. Mark APIs that need it with `[DynamicallyAccessedMembers]`, or prefer source generators, which produce ordinary code at compile time.

Generic attributes (C# 11) take type arguments: `[Validator<EmailRule>]`. Caller-information attributes (`[CallerMemberName]`, `[CallerArgumentExpression]`) let the compiler pass names and source text into parameters, which is how `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` reports parameter names.
Use reflection at boundaries (startup, configuration, tooling), cache what you discover, and check whether the app will be trimmed or AOT-compiled before depending on it.

challenge: Write a [Description("...")] attribute for enum members and a Describe(Enum value) helper that returns the description via reflection, or the member name when there is none. Test with an enum Level { [Description("Very low")] Low, High }.
question: Why is heavy reflection a problem for Native AOT and trimmed apps?
correct: The trimmer cannot see members used only via reflection and may remove them
wrong: Attributes are stripped by the C# compiler
reasoning: Annotate with DynamicallyAccessedMembers or replace reflection with source-generated code.
